Bill (No. 7) respecting the Inspection and Sale of Seeds-Mr. Fisher-was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon.
Is this the same Bill that was before the House last year and the year before?

Practically it is. There are, however, certain slight modifications which I shall explain in general terms. My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) who lias asked me this question, will remember that the Bill as introduced last session was for the purpose of controlling the sale of agricultural seeds, so as to remove a grievance or difficult}' which lias existed in the past, in that these seeds frequently are impure in having the seeds of weeds mixed with them, or in the seeds not being germinable, thus causing loss to the purchaser both in their purchase and in their use. For the purpose of learning the facts I instructed an officer in my department to investigate this question. As much as four years ago, this officer went carefully into the subject. He took a large number of samples of the seeds that were being sold in various parts of Canada and analyzed by methods well known in seed laboratories. His reports show that there was a real need for control over this trade. Investigation proved that large quantities of very inferior seeds were being sold in this country, and that in those seeds there was a large number of weed seeds, often the seeds of weeds that were unknown in the locality where the seed was to be fised, so that the result of its use would be to introduce into localities pernicious weeds which, till that time, had not been known in those localities. This was one part of the evil. The other part was that in frequent instances seed was sold under false names, that is, it was not what it was represented to be. A notorious instance of that kind was found in the eastern part of Canada, where a seed was sold purporting to be the seed of a spring grain, when, as a matter of fact, it was the seed of a grain which was to be sown in the fall in order to ripen. Again large quantities of seeds were sold of which a proportion, in some cases a considerable proportion, was not germinable. The purchaser, not knowing this, sowed the usual quantity and, of course, got little, if any, return. These difficulties in the trade were the more likely to' continue, because the farmer who purchased the seed had no means of determining its value. In some cases, of course, the weed seeds are quite apparent, but, not unfrequently, these seeds are not recognizable by the farmers. Sometimes they are seeds of weeds entirely unknown in the purchaser's locality, or in many cases, the farmer is not familiar with the seeds of even the ordinary weeds of his



own neighbourhood. In many other instances the value of the seed could not be determined except by what I might call laboratory methods, such as have been in established use for some time in other countries. In the United States and various European countries, the laboratory investigation of the quality and value of seeds has been carried on for . many years. There is to-day a thoroughly established method for the examination and testing of seeds of all kinds. We thought it wise that the advantages of science should be put within reach of the farmers of the Dominion of Canada for their protection in the seed trade. I therefore, established in the department a seed laboratory and the work of that labora- j tory has since been going on. I am glad to say that, by the testimony of the seedsmen themselves as well as of many farmers, the investigations and reports of this branch have contributed materially to improvement in the trade, and that for the last year or two there has been a decided improvement in the quality of the seeds sold to our farmers. A greater number of farmers to-day are critical of the seed they buy than formerly, and their knowledge has compelled improvement. But there is much yet to be done.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. There are many on this side anxious to hear the eloquence of the hon. minister and to follow his explanation, yet there is not an hon. gentleman on the ministerial side paying the slightest attention, and the noise of their conversation makes it impossible for us to hear the minister. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope lion, gentlemen will keep order for it is very unpleasant for a speaker to be interrupted.

The noise was not inter-ferring with me, Mr. Chairman, though I would prefer to talk without so much effort.
I need hardly say that I am not attempting any eloquence in regard to a matter of busi-nes such as this. I was saying that, though much had been accomplished there is still room for improvement. While the general average of the trade has been improved, I regret to say there are still in our country a number of men who handle seeds for agricultural purposes who do not seem to be alive to the importance of the trade and who still deal in very inferior seeds. This House has practically declared its opinion that a law should be passed to control this trade. A Bill was introduced last session, but was dropped because, owing to the lateness and length of the session, it was deemed impossible to make it law. I hope that, introducing it as I have done this session, at an early stage, when there is every opportunity for hon. members to give attention to the subject, the re-Mr. FISHER.
suit will be better. I think I can fairly call for the co-operation of members on both sides to effect this improvement in the relation of the farmers to those who supply them with seed, and that I may look with confidence to the Bill being passed into law. I shall be extremely disappointed if the Bill is not passed this session. I need hardly go into details in explaining the Bill, but may say in general terms that we wish to provide by this Bill machinery which will, in the first place prevent the sale of seed containing more than a certain number of seeds of pernicious weeds, the presence of the seeds of which, I consider, makes seed unfit to be sold in Canada. Section 3 and section 0 combined absolutely prohibit the sale of seeds containing certain weeds. In addition to that, we propose to establish a grade or standard of the seeds which shall be permitted to be sold with the brand of No. 1. or of an extra quality upon it. That is established by section 4. Then we propose to provide machinery by which the law may be carried out. I think, in brief language, I have given the substance of the Bill. The details will come up as the various sections are considered. I think perhaps it is better that I should defer the explanations of the changes that have been made in the present Bill as compared with the Bill of last session until we come to each section, when I will be able to explain more fully. Again I would repeat for the information of the House that the general proposals of the Bill are:	In the first place, to prohibit absolutely the sale of seed which contains seeds of particularly pernicious weeds; and secondly, to provide a standard, a No. 1 quality of seed.

We have had this same Bill before the House during two previous sessions. The first time, I understood, it was allowed to drop because it was found objectionable to seedsmen, and to farmers as well. Last year it was put on the paper at a reasonably early period of the session, and, of course, could have been put through if the government had made any effort to do so. Therefore, the minister and his side of the House are responsible for the Bill not going through last year. There was time enough, but it was assumed that so many objections were raised throughout the country that the government thought better not to push it on. Alight I ask whether, since then, the government have received numerous objections to the Bill, or whether reasons have been given why it should not pass, or amendments suggested. In my experience the seedsmen do not look upon it with much favour, whatever the farmers may think.

I think my hon. friend put the matter a little strongly when he alleged the reasons for the Bill not having been pxit through and made law last session. It is true the Bill was introduced about the mid-

die of die session, I think, but at the same time there was a great deal of other pressing matter before the House. Also certain: opposition to the Bill developed, chiefly on the part of the hon. gentlemen opposite, but on the part of a few gentlemen on this side of the House as well, who were afraid that the Bill might interfere unfairly with the trade. The seedsmen made certain objections. I do not remember, however, at the present time that any farmers' organization or any representative farmers intimated that there was anything in the Bill that they ob: jected to. On the contrary, I was able to quote and to show last session, and the session before, a very strong demand on the part of those organizations who in Canada largely speak for the farmers in a nonpolitical sense ; they wanted a Bill of this kind. The opposition which developed was raised chiefly at the instance of the seedsmen. But their objections were thoroughly threshed out last year, and related only to slight points which I have to a certain extent modified in the present Bill. But at the same time I do not profess to have met their views entirely, because if I did meet their views entirely I think the Bill would be practically emasculated, and would be of no use for the purpose of protecting farmers in the trade. I acknowledge that if this Bill did not tread upon the toes of somebody in the trade it would be unnecessary, and I would not have introduced it. It is only because there are certain people who deal in seeds in this country who require to be regulated by law that this Bill is necessary, and for that reason only am I desirous of making the Bill law. I speak of these people knowing well that they do not include the large majority of the seed dealers, who are an honourable body of men, who deal honestly and fairly, and carry on their trade in a reputable way. At the same time there are. unfortunately, certain other men dealing in seeds that ought not to be sold, and it is for the purpose of restraining these men that we find the necessity of this Bill. As I said a moment ago, when we come to the details of the measure I will be able to explain the slight modifications which I have made, and which will, I think, to a large extent meet the objections which some of the reputable traders in seeds expressed last session.

I think the minister, whether wittingly or unwittingly, does the opposition great injustice when he intimates that it was because of the opposition they (raised to the Bill that it was left over last session. The Bill was discussed, and after a lengthy discussion the opposition expected the Bill would go through. They had raised all the objections that they thought desirable to raise, and drew the minister's attention to the weak features of the Bill. After that they expected the Bill would be gone on with, and paid no more attention to it. But the government did not make any effort to lli
carry it through, the minister did not make any effort to carry his own Bill through. The reason which he gives to-day seems to me not to be a good one, that is to say, it was not pushed through because there was other more important business before the House for the government to deal with. According to the explanation which the hon. gentleman gave us at first he would seem to regard this measure as one of the most important which could be brought before this iHouse ; but if the interest of the farming community is to be staved off until every other measure and every other interest is attended to, and finally this Bill is to be thrown over, it seems to me that it is not very complimentary to the farmers. My first inquiry was as to whether this Bill was exactly the same as the previous Bills; also whether the hon. gentleman had received any objections to this Bill. If so, we can deal with them when we come to them.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the lion. Minister of Agriculture for some information in regard to' the extent of the weed plague, both in the eastern portion of the country and in the Northwest Territories. Is it a fact that there are more weeds in the west, especially in the wheat country, than formerly, and are they becoming a menace to the growth of wheat in that country ?

In regard to the latter part of my hon. friend's question, I think I am well within the mark in saying that as cultivation increases in the west the number of weeds increases. There is very little of what I might call hoe cultivation, practically none, and without that weeds are sure to increase wherever land is cultivated. They are increasing in that country just as cultivation is increasing. There is also a large introduction of weeds into the west in the crops which, before the land was cropped, .were entirely unknown. How they got there it is not easy to determine. In some cases they have been brought in in seed, and sometimes also they have lain dormant for many years, as weed seeds sometimes will, and are brought out by cultivation. In the eastern parts of Canada good culti-

vation, good farming, reduces the number of weeds. I would not like to say that in that respect our farmers are deteriorating. I think to-day there are more fields that are well cultivated in eastern Canada than there were fifteen or twenty years ago, but at the same time there is a spread of bad weeds in parts of the country where these individual and particular weeds were formerly unknown, and I think it is due to the greater facilities of communication and the greater facilities of trade, inasmuch as seeds that are grown in one part of the country are more often sent to another part of the country than they used to be in the.days of early settlement, when the farmers bought chiefly from their own neighbours and never went far away from home to get their seeds. To-day it is quite a common tiling for farmers in the older provinces of Canada to buy seed that has been grown hundreds of miles away from where it is to be sown. In the days of the early settlement this was not so much the case, and in consequence of this facility of trade new weeds are being found constantly in certain sections Of the country.

I would like to ask the hou. minister whether he can say there is any relation between the growth of the weed plague in the west and the change in the hard wheat belt. The hard wheat belt seems to be growing and the weed plague seems to be growing. I would ask him if he has any information on that point?
I do not think I have. I do not know of any information that would lead me to believe that the presence of weeds in the soil or the growth of weeds in the crop has affected the quality of the wheat.
But the hard wheat belt is moving. It does not remain in the same place.
I will accept the hon. gentleman's statement. I do not know whether it is true or not.

As one interested in the seed trade for a number of years, I would like to submit a few observations in connection with this clause. I would call attention first to the latter part of the first paragraph of clause 3.
Unless each and every receptacle, package, sack or bag containing such seeds, or a label securely atached thereto, is marked in plain and indelible manner, &e.
I would submit that packages are of different sizes, and that what might be quite
possible in regard to a 200 weight package will be quite impossible in connection with a very small package. The Bill as now framed makes no difference between packages of different size, but the small dealer buys some of his seeds in very small quantities. It would be impossible to put the names of all the noxious weeds on one of these packages as they are not large enough. *In this list there are 25 names, many of which are long and unintelligible to the average farmer. It seems to me that if we are going to have a law of this kind it should be a practical law and one that could be carried out. As a merchant who has been engaged in the handling of seeds, I would like to be in a position to assist in the carrying of legislation which is practical, but I do not think from my experience that all of these names can be put on each receptacle or bag. There is no way in the average seed warehouse of printing all of these names and they would have to be written, which would be a serious matter because sometimes a merchant will have from 100 to 200 packages of seed on hand; to label every one of these packages seems unnecessary so long as the particular package from which the merchant is selling is labelled, in order that the buyer will know what he is buying, which ought to be the principal thing required. There is no intention* on the part of the average merchant to impose on the public seeds that are not fit for sale or use, and I think the seed merchants are as much entitled to respect in this regard as other merchants. They endeavour to do what is right and expect to do business because of the confidence people have in them.
What I cannot understand in- subsection 2 of subsection 3 is why farmers are exempted from tlie legislation which is applied to merchants. Seed that may be purchased from one farmer by another may be as harmful as any seed purchased from a merchant. If the seed sold by the farmer is as noxious as that sold by the merchant, the farmer should be under the same law as the merchant, but according to this subsection, he does not seem to be ; he may sell to his neighbour seed which a merchant would be prohibited from selling. That is one law for the merchant and another for the farmer. I come from a section where seed growing is a considerable business and our farmers are anxious to have their seed placed on the market. If it cannot be so placed then so much money will be tied up in bags, because the law says that the grain cannot be sold as seed as it may contain too much of these weeds.
I submit that these criticisms ought to have the attention of the minister. I regret that the Bill is in my hands now for the first time and that I have not had the pleasure of hearing it discussed before and I would like to have some opportunity of looking into its provisions. I desire to co-

operate with the minister in any way I can, hut I submit that some of these features are impracticable, and I think that we should endeavour to have all legislation that we may pass carried out in the spirit in which it is enacted.

I may tell my hon. friend (Mr. Cockshutt) that I quite concur in his idea that the law should be such as can be carried out easily for the seller as well as the buyer. I have framed the provisions of this Act with that idea always in view, and I think that practically the Act does allow all of that. My hon. friend has made three criticisms of this section which I shall take up one by one. His first criticism is that it will be practically impossible for the seller to put all the names of these weeds on the packages. I may say to my hon. friend frankly that I consider that this section will practically prohibit a seller selling seed with these weeds in it. If he does undertake to sell seed with the names of these seeds on it, and says that they are all in that seed, I do not think that any farmer will buy it. If he is selling seed which contains a majority of the weeds mentioned in that list he ought not to sell it because he will be selling something which will be disgraceful to this trade ; he should be prevented from doing it. It is possible that a man might honestly and properly sell seed containing one or two of those weeds,' and in order to enable that to be done with proper protection to the trade, I have changed the original intention of the Bill as introduced two years ago, when the sale of seed containing any of these weed seeds was to be absolutely prohibited. The Bill in its present form does permit of a little safeguard for the honest seller who may know that there are some of these seeds, a very few, in the seeds they are selling, and who then honestly tell their purchasers of this fact. That provision is made distinctly and directly in the interests of the trade, allowing them to go as far in the way of selling seed containing seeds of these pernicious weeds as I think it would be proper and right to permit.
My hon. friend speaks of the size of the package. These weed seeds would not be in the garden seeds which are sold in small packages such as my hon. friend perhaps has in his mind's eye when he speaks as he has done. A great many garden seeds are sold in little paper packages on which it would be difficult to write the names of these weeds, but we do not expect to find these weeds in these seeds, and if they were in them it would be highly improper and we should do anything we can to prevent it. If a package is large enough to have a label attached to it bearing the name, surname and address of the seller and the name of the variety of the seed contained in it, it would be possible to write on the back of the label the names of the weeds whose Mr. COCKSHUTT.
seeds are contained in it, and there would be no real difficulty in that. If we allow what my hon. friend proposes we would have a condition of affairs under which the farmer would purchase his seed and have it taken perhaps by a scoop out of a large bag or box in the store of the salesman, and afterwards if he found that that seed was not good or if he took a sample of it to be tested by the seed laboratory, it would be impossible for him to prove conclusively that that seed had come out of any individual package or bag or box in the seed salesman's warehouse, and therefore there would be no possibility of proceeding against the salesman.
In regard to the second objection which the hon. gentleman made, that clause 2 of subsection 2, of section 3, seems to exempt farmers from the provisions of this Act. I may say that it only exempts farmers from the provisions of this particular section. The reason for that exemption is this : As my hon. friend says, we do not wish to interfere with the trade of anybody, and more than is absolutely necessary. The provisions of this section are very limited, because they apply only to the case of a farmer who sells seed on his own premises to somebody who is going to use the seed, not to sell again, but for seeding purposes. Practically it exempts the case of a farmer who on his own soil sells seed which he has grown himself on that very soil to a neighbouring farmer who is going to sow it. That does not offend against one principle of this Act, which is intended to prevent the spread of weed seeds in new sections. The farmer does not send it away somewhere pise to be used. In the next place, the farmer who purchases the seed probably knows the land of the farmer who raised it-knows whether it is clean land, knows pretty well what kind of weeds were growing in that farmer's fields, and he purchases the seed with his eyes open to all these things; whereas if the farmer buys seed from the seed merchant, he does net know where the seed was grown, has never seen the fields where ic was grown, does not know whether they were clean or not, does not know whether the seed came from a thousand miles away or from the next farm, and therefore does not know what evil weeds he may be introducing into his own farm and his own section. The two cases are entirely different. It is for the purpose of preventing an unnecessary interference with the sale and purchase of seeds among neighbours where seed is largely grown that this proviso and exemption is made. But the exception is very small, because if the purchaser chooses, he may require that the seed be sold under the provisions of the Act. If he does not require that, he purchases the seed with his eyes open without availing himself of the protection which this Act provides. This

clause is only put In for the purpose of facilitating trade in seeds amongst neighbours, and not unnecessarily interfering with that part of the seed trade. But the trade with seed merchants is so totally different that it requires a supervision and control which the other class of trade does not.

The non. gentleman meets to a certain extent the objection which I made, hut still I think not fully, with regard to the sale of seed by one farmer to another. The merchant is deprived of the sale of such seed, and at the same time is hampered with legislation, while the farmer is not. Therefore, he cannot take advantage of the facilities of the Act and do the business he could do. without it. The average profit on a bushel of clover seed is only about five per cent of its value, which constitutes a valid reason why it is not fair to hamper the merchant. It should be remembered that the merchant is not the originator of the seed; but the farmer or grower is. When the farmer takes the seed to market, the buyer may say to him, I must send the seed to the laboratory at Ottawa and ascertain whether it is saleable under the Act; if it is not, I must leave it on your hands. If the merchant practices adulteration, you can punish him; but if he buys from a farmer in good faith and offers the seed for sale in good faith, he is dealing in a fair and honourable way, even though he may not be living up to the strict terms of the Act. The secret of the whole matter is that the farmer is the grower of the seed in the first place, and therefore the Bill should begin with the land. The man who grows the seed is the best judge of what is in it. He knows whether the field is thoroughly clean or whether it is infested with wild oats or mustard, for instance. 1 would rather have two minutes to look over the field where the seed is grown than an hour to examine bag after bag of the seed. Therefore, I think the grower of the seed should be held accountable rather than the merchant or handler of the seed. The merchant should not be hampered more than the farmer is. Both should come under the one law. If the merchant is held amenable to it, so should be the farmer, who in selling to his neighbour is taking away from the merchant the business which he would otherwise have. The merchant has to pay taxes, and he, should be safeguarded in his business. I submit these points for the consideration of the minister.

My hon. friend has completely endorsed what I said a moment ago, that in such a sale as X referred to, the purchaser does not need the protection of this Act. The hon. gentleman said he would rather have two minutes to examine the field where the seed was grown than an hour or two to examine bag after bag of the seed. That is just what the purchaser does who
buys seed on the premises where it is grown, and therefore he does not need the protection which the farmer does who buys from the seed merchant. But my hon. friend forgets another thing. The seed sold by the farmer must be sold to another farmer for his own use. The seed merchant buys from the farmer who grows the seed, and then cleans the seed. He has appliances and facilities for cleaning it, and as a matter of fact the seedmen of Canada do clean their seed. Further on, the Bill allows the farmer to sell seed to the seed merchant for cleaning purposes. In section 7, there is a provision that if the seed is sold to the merchant to be cleaned, then the provisions of the Act do not apply. The merchant buys from the farmer the poor or dirty seed, and proceeds to clean it and sell it as clean seed. He pays the farmer a much less price for the dirty seed than he receives for the clean seed which he sells, and quite rightly, for he ought to be paid for his work of cleaning it. But it is not necessary that the provisions of the Act should apply where a farmer sells impure or dirty seed to a merchant to be cleaned. The merchant can take care of himself quite well.
'Mr. A. A. WRIGHT. I wish to say one word with reference to this Bill. It came before our farmers' institute a year ago, and there was only one objection which the farmers had to it. It was this, that it prevented the farmers from trading in seed among themselves. You know that a farmer who lives on clay land is always anxious to buy seed from his neighbour who lives on sharp or sandy soil. He thinks that the seed grown upon sharp soil, when sowed upon clay land, would produce a better crop, and that the seed grown upon clay land, when sown upon sharp soil, will produce equally good results. Frequently farmers are anxious to exchange their labour for seed and cannot go to a merchant to buy it. Farmers should have tiie privilege of buying seed from one another without getting into any difficulty under this Act. They buy with their eyes open. An examination of the field when the crop is growing gives a far better idea of the quality of the seeds than looking at the crop after it is harvested and threshed. Consequently, the farmers are anxious that the Bill should be changed so that they might be free to purchase from one another. As regards 'the marking of packages, no one would ever buy seeds which would have on the package the names of all these weeds, and no man would undertake to put up packages of seed for sale which would contain all these foul seeds.

How will this section affect merchants in the country districts who buy grain from the farmers ? Suppose a merchant buys a lot of grain and the very same day sells a number of packages of the seeds which turn out to contain some foul weeds,

would the merchant be subject to the penalty provided by this Act ?

The exception in this clause only applies to the purchaser who buys front a farmer for the purpose of using the seed hiihself. If the seed is sold to a man who wishes to sell again, all the provisions of the Aet apply.
In many cases the merchants have no way of knowing whether there are foul seeds in the grain purchased or not.
If they undertake to deal in seeds, they must take the necessary precautions to secure pure seeds.

How can a country grain dealer, who buys seeds from a farmer and probably the very same day sells some of those seeds, tell whether there are any foul seeds in the grain or not ? I do not see why you should bring him under the provisions of the Act. In allowing one farmer to sell foul seeds to another, you are placing a bonus on the spreading by farmers of foul seeds in the neighbourhood where they live.

If the local grain dealer buys seed from a farmer, all the provisions of the Act apply to the farmer who sells to him. It is only when a farmer sells to another farmer who intends using the seed for sowing purposes, that the exemption applies. If a farmer sells to a country store-keeper, the store-keeper has the same recourse against the farmer as the farmer would have against him. But if a farmer sells to a merchant, who has cleaning machinery, grain for the purpose of being cleaned. then the provisions of the Act do not apply to the farmer. P.ut if he sells to a purchaser, who intends selling the seed again without cleaning it, then the farmer comes under the Act.

In our section of the . country, the farmers often sell without knowing what the purchaser intends doing with the grain. The purchaser does not let the farmer know that he is buying the grain to sell it as seed. Suppose a farmer sells grain to a grain dealer and then the grain dealer sells some of the grain to another farmer who wants it for seed, in what position would the farmer in the first instance be ? He did not sell the grain to the purchaser in order that the purchaser might sell it again. He sold it that the purchaser might do as he likes with it.
That would be a matter left to the discretion of the court and the court in such case would probably find the farmer guiltless and the grain merchant guilty.

It seems to me that the object of the Bill is. to a considerable extent, Mr. WALSH.
to furnish grist to the lawyers. The usual custom is for the farmer to sell his grain wherever he finds the best market. Surely there should be a guarantee given the farmer that he did or did not sell the grain for seed. Otherwise the merchant can throw the responsibility back upon the farmer and endless litigation would be the result. There should be some provision to protect the farmer or he will be in continual trouble. No doubt where a seed grower has grown grain for seed, where he has exhibited it for sale as seed, it is necessary that the law should protect the purchaser against the purchase of foul seeds. But when a farmer sells grain without understanding that it is purchased to be sold again as seed, why should he be responsible? A country merchant, purchasing grain from a farmer might ask if he could sell the grain for seed. The farmer, not understanding the law-it would take a long time to understand it-gives his consent, and sells his grain at the best price he can get for it. The merchant can afterwards plead that he purchased the grain for seed and so paid a high price, and, if proceeded against under the law, might throw the responsibility on the farmer. I submit that the farmer, selling his grain in that way must be given better protection than he is given under this Bill.

I sympathize with my hon. friend's (Mr. Barr's) desire to protect both sides of the bargain, and I think this Bill does protect botli sides to the utmost possible extent. My hou. friend says that a country store-keeper buying grain from a farmer can afterwards sell it for seed and pretend that he bought it for seed from the farmer. But the machinery of the Bill, which we come to later on, provides that, in order to be able to make such a plea the purchaser must within seven days take a sample and have it analyzed, and, if the seed is found to be impure or wrongly described, the purchaser must proceed against the farmer from whom he bought the seed for having sold it under false representation. I think this completely protects both sides in the case we are discussing. But I say frankly that I do not want the farmer or the country store-keeper, or the seed merchant either, to be protected so much that we never can convict him if he has done wrong. I want the Bill such that under it wrong-doing can be punished and so prevented. My hon. friend seems to fear that the farmers or country store-keepers will not be informed about the law. As soon as it becomes law I intend to take every means in my power to spread the knowledge of it, as I did with regard to tlie proposals for this Bill, concerning which the farming community are pretty well informed, as well as concerning the discussion of the subject in this House last year. I think the leading farmers, at any rate in

B11 sections of the country, as well as the country store-keepers and the seed merchants are pretty well informed as to what is proposed in this Bill. And they will he still better informed if it becomes law.

I would like to ask the minister what position the millers will be in under this law? Speaking for my own city of Chatham, I can say that the millers there take every precaution to get. the best seed to dispose of among the farmers. And the same is true of the seed merchants. It seems to me that the effect of this Bill will be to drive a great many dealers out of business and so put the farmers at a disadvantage.

Anybody who sells seed for seed purposes will come under the operation of the Bill whether he is a miller, a dealer, a farmer or anything else-except the farmer who sells on his own premises to his neighbour. My hon. friend (Mr. Clements) describes in eulogistic terms the seedsmen and millers of his district and I have no doubt lie describes them truly. These people need not fear the Bill; on the contrary it is a Bill that will protect them from dishonest competition.

It seems to me that the millers will be compelled to go out of the selling of wheat, oats and things of that kind as seed. Yet, I am sure hon. members will agree with me that millers throughout the country are most anxious to furnish the farmers with the best seed possible and that they do it.
If they are selling seed that will render them liable to prosecution, they are selling seed that it is not desirable that the farmers should buy.

I would call the hon. minister's attention to a rather different phase of subsection 2 from that we have been discussing. The argument has been directed to the idea that the farmers are getting too much indulgence under this section. On the other hand, I think they are not getting the protection they are entitled to. It is true that there is a provision which may, to some extent, facilitate the disposal of their grain by the farmers-But when we turn to section 7, it appears to me-and I would ask the minister to take it into his consideration before we pass that section finally-that, the farmer should have the protection that is thrown about him under subsection 2 not only as regards selling to a neighbouring farmer, but in all cases. In one case, he is selling his grain not knowing to what purpose it will be diverted, and in the other he is selling it knowing that it will be used for seed. To avoid the possibility of lawsuits and the complications that would follow, I submit, the subsection should be framed in such a way as to afford protection to the farmer in all cases of selling bis grain ; and should
throw on the dealer in seeds the onus of seeing that the grain is uot resold for seed until it is put in proper condition. That could be accomplished, perhaps, by the introduction of a very few words. I will read the section as I would like to see it, for the consideration of the minister :
The provisions contained in this section shall not apply to the sale of seed grown, sold and delivered by any farmer on his own premises, for seeding by the purchaser himself or to a dealer in seeds, unless the purchaser himself or the dealer in the seeds obtains from the seller at the time of the sale thereof a certificate that the seed is supplied to him subject to the provisions of this Act.
The proper course is to provide that dealers in seeds shall guarantee to the public that seeds purchased from them are in reasonable condition, and to leave the farmer absolutely free to sell his seed to a dealer in whatever condition it may he, because, the farmer has not facilities, pro; bably, to extract the various weed-seeds, and. in many instances is not aware of the fact that these objectionable seeds are present in tlie grain.

Would the minister say what would he the probable cost to a seedsman of the machinery necessary to clean all the seeds he has referred to? I cannot help thinking that if the machinery is expensive it will not only increase the cost of the seed to the farmer, but it will ' place the seed business in the control of a very few hands.	,

The cost of the machinery to clean the seed would depend altogether upon its capacity as well as upon its effectiveness. Probably the largest seed dealers in Canada have machinery whicli would fulfil all the requirements of this Act, and sufficient to meet all the demands likely to j be made upon them. Such a machine would ; cost about $800 ; while for a small business, an ordinary fanning mill would do a: great deal, though it would not be completely effective, such a machine as can he got for $30 or $40. But the large seed merchants could get ail the machinery required in this country, for less than $1,000.

Then I think the effort will be practically to force the cleaning of seeds and the sale of seeds, in our country, into the hands of a comparatively few. There are very few local seed merchants who would invest in machinery costing $800 for the purpose of cleaning the seed that will be sold in their community. While I think that many provisions in the Bill, are wise, there are others that I think are too sweeping. When you compel farmers to purchase only such seeds as have gone through the hands of the seed merchants, you may depend upon it they are going to pay a great deal more for their seeds.

As a matter of fact, the seed merchants of Canada to-day are pretty well equipped with seed cleaning machinery, The seed merchants have practically all the machinery necessary to fulfil the requirements of this Act. An investment in a plant costing from $500 to $700 or $800 to enable a man to carry on a business of this kind, would be a very small charge ' upon the business. When it comes to the farmers themselves cleaning their ; seeds, they cannot do it ; therefore we provide machinery by which, under certain conditions and in certain circumstances, they can sell seeds if the purchaser chooses to buy from them.
How many seed merchants have the necessary machinery V
Is there one between Kingston and Toronto ?
I am told by my officer who is familiar with the trade that there are fully fifteen seed merchants who have the full equipment.
Is that for the whole Dominion ?

That is a big combine.
Mi-. FISHER. That would be for the whole Dominion, but most of them are located in the province of Ontario.

What will Manitoba and the other provinces that have no machinery, of this kind do ? It is not likely to benefit the farmer, and that is the starting point. It seems to me dangerous legislation and is making a radical change.

There are two or three seed merchants in the province of Manitoba who are thoroughly equipped, and one at any rate in the province of British Columbia who is well equipped ; and there are some others in Ontario further east.

The point raised by my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) was exactly the point I wanted to bring to the notice of the minister. While I would compliment the minister upon his desire to pass useful legislation in this direction, I cannot see myself that it is going to benefit the farming community to any extent. It will certainly cause a great deal of trouble.

So far as my experience goes, no machine has yet been devised that can thoroughly remove all the seeds named in the Bill, and that is the point I desire to draw to the attention of the minister. For instance, from alsike clover and timothy seed there is no machine yet devised that can remove false flax seed. So far as I am aware that has never been removed successfully by any machine.

Now the minister rather intimated that seed merchants wilfully left in certain seeds that might be removed by machinery. I believe it is the endeavour of every honest merchant to remove every impure seed that it is possible for him to remove. But I want to point out that there are certain seeds mentioned in this Bill that cannot be removed by any machine ever yet designed. No machine can be designed, unless it has eyes that can take out those weed seeds that are the same size and weight as the pure seed. Wind won't do it, and sieves won't do it. Then what will do it ? Nothing bpt eyes, and we have no machine yet. that has eyes and that will take out these seeds of similar weight and similar size, and only different colour, from the sample. The effect of the Bill will be to put the business into a few hands, to raise immensely to the farmers of this country both the price of the seed grain and the seed grasses ; and both of these, if they are cheap, constitute an element of wealth that no farmer can afford to ignore. My belief is that clover seed at $8 or $10 a bushel is quite high enough ; if you put it up to $12 or $14 a bushel you are going to do great harm to agriculture in this country. I submit it is not well to pass too drastic a measure. I trust tlie minister will allow that clause to stand until he has had an opportunity to look into it and to make it more workable.

I would point out to my hon. friend that I did not say that weed seeds would be entirely removed; I said that machinery was in existence which could conform to the provisions of this Act. The provisions of this Act do not require absolute purity, they come as closely to it as we can make them under the circumstances prevailing in the trade. We do not expect to get absolute purity, we would be very glad to do so, but that is likely to be impossible. 1 may say that the Bill has been considerably modified so as to make it less stringent than the Bill of last session. But I desire to say that if the Bill is not passed as stringent as it is here framed, it will be practically useless in improving the seed trade in this country ; and I am not prepared to take the responsibility of leaving the seed trade any longer without control.

I am inclined to think that if the seed trade got into fewer hands it would be better for the farmers of this country, because the dealers would be able to get a better class of seed and sell it cheaper than they would otherwise. Allow me to give you one illustration from my own riding. A gentleman from the state of New York came there and went into the seed business. When he was purchasing seed he got a list of all the farmers who grew good seed. He had an agent whom he sent round to inspect every field before the crop was harvested, so that lie

might know exactly what foul seed of any kind was growing in that field. When he found farmers who had the very best quality of seed and the cleanest fields, it was from them he purchased his seed. The consequence was that farmers gradually began to grow a better class of seed. But unfortunately the duty imposed by the United States government on seeds going into that country was so high that he could not export any from Canada. I think, therefore, that if this Bill becomes law we will eventually have not only better seed, but cheaper seed, by reason of the inspection of seeds in the fields where they are growing.
What kind of seed is it that the hon. gentleman refers to?
Peas.
It is a great trouble to clean peas I am sure. You must have time. An ordinary fanning mill would take all the foul seeds out of peas.

On section 4,
