No person shall sell, or offer, expose or have in his possession for sale, any seeds of timothy, red clover, alsike, or any mixture containing the said seeds, in or from any receptacle, package, sack or bag upon which is marked ' No. 1 ' or any other designation which represents such seeds as of first quality, unless they are free from the seeds of weeds named in section 3 of this Act, and are also free form the seeds of Whi-te Cockle, (Lychnis vespertina, (Sibth.) ; Night-Flowering Catch-fly, (Silene noctiflora, L.) ; False Flak, (CameJinB. satliva, Cirautx.); Oanad|a Thistle, (Onieus anvensds, HoffmO ; Ox-eye, Daisy, (Chrysanthemum Leucanthemum, L.) ; Curled Dock. (Rumex Crispus, L.) ; Blue Weed, (Eehium ivulgaife, iL.) ; Ri-bg-ras-si: (Plantago lanceolata, L.) ; Chicory, (Cichorium Intybus, L.), and contain out of every one hundred seeds not less than ninety-nine seeds of the kind or kinds represented, or seeds of other useful and harmless grasses and clovers, of which ninety-nine seeds must be germinable.

I would call the bon. minister's attention to this in connection with the next section. Probably we could deal with it when we come to section 5, but we might as well understand bow it works out now. It is provided that out of every one hundred seeds ninety-nine shall be of the kind or kinds proposed to be sold. Then, section 5 provides :
The .Governor in Council may make regulations determining the maximum proportion of seeds of the. weeds named in sections 3 and 4 of this Act, that may he tolerated in any seeds without affecting their character as being within the meaning of the -said sections free from the seeds of the said weeds.
I do not see how these two sections can possibly work out together. There is a definite provision in section 4 that out of
every hundred seeds ninety-nine must be of the character proposed to be sold. If that is absolute then the provision contained in section 5 can have no application ; and it is very important, I should think,
! that there should be some provision of that | character because it is almost impossible that i the growers of seeds should come up to the provision which is here contained, if I understand these two sections aright.
- Mr. FISHER. In reply to my hon. friend I will say that section 4 is absolute. Of every one hundred seeds there must be ninety-nine of the kind which is purported to be sold. But, the regulations winch may be passed under section 5 could not contravene that in any way whatever. That would refer to the percentage of seeds which might be allowed where the Act requires that the sample must lie free from seeds, but that would in no way override the necessity of ninety-nine seeds out of a hun-\ dred being true to the name of. the sample.

Does the hon. minister see the effect of that ? Is it possible to work that out in the. way the bon. minister suggests ? It is provided that out of every one hundred seeds there shall be ninety-nine of the character that is purported to be sold ; that is that out of oue hundred seeds in the whole package there shall be ninety-nine seeds of the character represented to be sold. Then w^bat happens under section 5 ? That only allows one per cent of objectionable seeds. That only leaves oue per cent of all those w7eed seeds enumerated in section 3 and again added to in section 4, which may be represented in these seeds. Then, how can it be worked out ? The Governor in Council may determine what proportion of objectionable seeds shall be iu a package without militating against the provisions of the Act. That-I say it with all due respect-is not good sense upon the face of it.

I do not agree with my hon. friend. If my hon. friend will look at .section 6 he will see that there is a provision in that section also for a greater proportion than five to one thousand of the seeds sold as being permissible even though the Act may say that no weed seeds shall be present. Now, the regulations under section 5 may go as high as ten per thousand permissible and still not interfere with the provision of one per cent in section 4, but they may go a great deal less than ten per thousand. They may by regulation be placed at only two or three per thousand and that would not contravene or interfere with the one per cent which may under section 4 be existent. But section 4 requires absolutely that there shall be ninety-nine per cent of the seed which is purported to be sold ; that is absolute and no regulation under section 5 can go beyond that or allow more than one per cent,

but it might allow mnoli less than the one per cent and still be within the provision of the Act.
Which is only making it a little more absurd than I thought it was. That is all the difference.
I cannot see it.

It comes down to this, according to the hon. minister and according to the section, that the utmost, of foul seed that can be contained in the package is one per cent, but after providing for that condition of things and after the admission, extracted by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) that as to certain seeds it is impossible to extract them, we have this position of things that the most that can possibly be contained in a package is one per cent of foul seeds. Then we have sections 5 and 6 containing this additional provision that the Governor in Council may make regulations by which the one per cent of foul seeds shall not be permitted. What condition of things will we have in regard to the farmer who is growing seeds ? 1 am not solicitous about other parties because I think they caq protect themselves, but we have this condition as regards the farmers that we have them reduced to the absolute necessity of having ninety-nine per cent of the kind of seeds that are purported to be sold, with the additional burden, cast upon them, that the Governor in Council may make a regulation that even that door of one per cent of escape may be closed and it may be made a fraction of one per cent, if it was unreasonable before, I think it is much more unreasonable by reason of these provisions contained in sections 5 and (3.
I do not think my hon. friend understands the section.
That is the trouble.

Yes, that is the trouble, but at the same tim.e as the trouble is there, I will try to explain it. Under section 4 there are two conditions which are requisite before a sample of seeds can be marked No. 1. The first is that the seeds are free from the seeds of certain weeds. Does my hon. friend understand that ?
Y'es.

First, that they are free from the seeds of the weeds named. That is the first condition. The. second condition is that there shall be at least ninety-nine seeds in every one hundred of the seed *which is purported to be sold. Now, in regard to the first condition, the Governor in Council may make regulations as to what percentage, if I may call it so, or fraction of a percentage may be permitted and the sample still be considered to be free from these weed seeds. That would probably Mr. FISHER.
be, surely be in this case, far less than one per cent permissible.
Exactly, it must be.
Then in regard to the second contention of its being necessary that 99 seeds out of 100 should be the seed's purporting to be sold, section 5 does not apply to that at all.	.
No, I know that.

Very well then, as far as the first part of it is concerned, it would state what number of seeds per thousand were allowed to be present without being considered to be present. That may sound like an anomaly, that they are present but yet are not to be considered present ; but that is in deference to what my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) has pointed out-and I was well aware of it-that we do not expect absolute perfection, we do not expect to get absolute freedom from all weed seeds, but we do want to get just as little as the conditions of the trade, the perfection of machinery and circumstances will permit. We have, therefore, inserted section 5 for the purpose of making a slight allowance for human fallability and weakness, or for the weakness of machinery, if you choose to put it in that way. I think my hon. friend will now understand the necessity of the two sections.

I think I understand the minister. It is just this, that there must be 99 seeds out of each 100 which are seeds of the variety purporting to be sold. There may be one foul seed in 100, but that possibility does not become absolute, because the Governor in Council may cut that down just as much as they like.

My hon. friend does not go quite far enough. What he says is true of the seeds named, but there might be other seeds which are not named, and still there must not be more than one per cent of weed seeds.

The minister says that there is only one per cent of margin. In any case there must be 99 per cent of pure seed ; if there are other seeds that are not named here, there is still only one per cent to work on. I would ask the minister if he thinks it is wise to make so drastic a provision in reference to this matter, and to throw such a serious onus on the people who raise and sell seeds ?

My hon. .friend again misses one point: this is optional. A man need not put ' No. 1 ' on a package. This is a clause which provides, that if a package of seeds is sold as No. 1, that is, as the best quality, it must live up to this clause. If a man is selling seed that he knows is not No. 1, he should not put No. 1 on his seed.

That is what I wanted to get at. I quite admit that it is optional,

but vliat I want to ensure is that the sale of what may be safely branded as No. 1 seed shall not be confined to the hands of half a dozen men. This Act Is driving out of the market the large class of producers, and is confining the market to the hands of the half dozen men who have this superior machinery, and when you limit it so that the requirement is as near perfection as you can get-as near perfection as the late Ontario government, ' almost perfection '- you are driving out the producers and the honest, hard working farmer, and creating a monopoly in the hands of a few, which thing is what I want to avoid.

I am rather disposed to take straight issue with the hon. gentleman. If it is necessary that the farmer, in order to get good seed, should have to get it from only a few people. I think that is better for the farmer than to get bad seed from a lot of people. I am prepared to pass a law so drastic that if people will not live up to the law and give the farmers what they profess to be selling to them, they shall he driven out of business. That is the whole purpose of the law. As I said, to begin with, if this Rill did not tread upon the toes of any one in the seed business, there would not be any raison d'etre for the Bill at all.
What ?
Does my hon. friend dispute that ? Perhaps he wants a translation.
You ought to talk so that people will understand you.
The hon. gentleman understands ; he read some French the other day.
I did not recognize the French.
The hon. gentleman's ear and pronunciation are so perfect in that language that I bow to his superior knowledge. We had an evidence of it the other day.
Humbug.

I say frankly that I do not want seed to be sold as No. 1 which will not live up to the provisions of this section. I am prepared to advocate that the Bill should be so drastic that seed cannot be sold to farmers in Canada marked as ; No. 1 ' and said to be of the highest quality, unless it lives up to the provisions of this section. As a matter of fact, we have had a large number of samples of seed tested, and I have here a statement of what was collected last year. We collected 450 samples through the country, and of the timothy seed 49 per cent of the samples lived up to the provisions of this section; of alsike seed, 17 per cent lived up to the provisions of the section ; and of red clover, 21 per cent, and. these were samples of seed that were taken largely in the parts of Canada where avowedly poor seed is sold. When we come to
take the samples of seed sent to us by reliable and responsible merchants, we find that there were 196 samples received. Of the samples of timothy 76 per cent were up to this standard ; alsike, 54 per cent: and of red clover, 63 per cent, showing that if men try to carry on their business properly and rightly, there is no difficulty for them to be able to live up to the provisions of this section. It can be done if people will only try to do it, and if they will not try to do it, it is the object of this Bill to make them do it.
Will the minister tell us what number of firms in western Ontario have the necessary machinery for cleaning the seeds-machinery which costs over $800 ?

I would not like to mention the names of the firms ; to do it would look a little too much like advertising. I may say that a considerable number of the leading seed merchants in Ontario have the machinery.
As there are only fifteen in the Dominion, would it do any harm to name them all ?
I do not think it would be wise to name individual firms.

It seems to me that one of the great difficulties in the discussion of this Bill is the manner in which the Bill is drawn. If I understand it correctly, the intention of section 4 is that there is to be not more than one seed out of 100 that is not the right kind of seed. If that is the manner in which this is to he judged, I see absolutely no use of clause 5, which says the Governor in Council may determine how many poor seeds may be tolerated. It says that distinctly-
The Governor in Council may make regulations determining the maximum proportion of seeds of the weeds named in sections 3 and 4 of this Act.
I understood the minister to say that it did not mean the seeds named in section 3, but it might mean some other seed. I think this Bill is not properly drawn for presentation to this House.

I am sorry to hear the hon. gentleman's opinion on such a subject. I venture to say that the Bill is drawn by the best draftsmen of Bills that are available for this House or this country. I do not pretend myself to draft Bills. They are drawn by the Department of Justice, on the instruction we give as to what is required. But I think I have given a complete explanation of the point at issue, and have shown that clause 5 does not apply at all to the percentage of foreign seeds, in what my hon. friend has quoted in section 4.
Wliat do you 'want It in for ?

Because it applies to another portion of section 4. As I stated a few minutes ago, there are two conditions in clause 4, and clause 5 regulates or controls to a certain extent the first condition, but does not interfere in any way with the second condition. My hon. friend who spoke a few minutes ago insists that it does. I cannot help it if he does not understand it.
As a plain, practical farmer, I wish to say that there is the trouble. The minister says he is pleading for the poor farmer. Well, I am one of them.
My hon. friend is not a poor farmer.

I made my Jiving as a farmer, which you never did. If the hon. gentleman does not understand farming better than he does this Bill, he would be in a very humble position in life if he tried to make his living by it. He tells the farmers that they can understand this Bill thoroughly. If it is so plain, how is it that the Minister of Agriculture, with all his wisdom, cannot explain it so that the lawyers of this House can understand it ? What position will the poor farmer be in w7hen he goes before a court? I want to impress this on the hon. gentleman's mind- because it requires a great deal to impress a fact on the mind of a gentleman who is so conceited that he thinks he knows it all- that this Bill is so complicated that with all his explanations he cannot bring it down to the comprehension of the lawyers of this House. I wonder if the Minister of Justice understands the Bill that he has drafted.

I want to draw attention to the word ' free ' used in clause 4. I understood the hon. minister to say, when discussing clause 3, that he did not expect absolute purity; but the word ' free ' as used in clause 4, is not a comparative term; it is absolute, so that if there is one impure seed in a bushel it cannot be said to be free. That is an impossibility. There must be absolute purity from all the seeds enumerated in clause 3, and also those named in clause 4.

No, no. That is just why I want clause 5, to which another hon. gentleman objects so much, so that we may make a regulation to provide that absolute freedom to a certain extent as it may be found necessary.
On section 7-exemptions from the Act,
Why should the provision for cleaning seeds be confined to merchants ? It seems to me that the farmers should be included. A cleaning machine costing $800 might be purchased and taken
around from farmer to farmer in the same way as is done with a threshing machine.
If the seeds were cleaned in the way my hon. friend suggests, by the farmers themselves, they would not be sold at all until after they were cleaned; and then they would not require to be exempted.

If the Minister of Agriculture took steps to educate the farmers as to the different kinds of seeds, he might encourage them to prevent the spread of noxious weeds without embarrassing them so much. If he had sample cases prepared, such as I think he has already prepared, with noxious seeds contained in small bottles, properly labelled, and if every seed merchant were compelled to have one of these cases on exhibition at the place where he sold seeds, and at the same time have a bottle containing the seeds he was selling absolutely free from impurities, so that the farmers could see them, he might in that way do a great deal to educate them without hampering them, and prevent a great deal of litigation.

I am glad to hear the suggestion of my hon. friend. We have been trying to do that kind of work. We have had prepared a cardboard box containing samples of the weed seeds known in the country and are distributing those boxes to those who deal in seeds and the agricultural organizations throughout the country. That is one of the educational factors that we have been making use of in order to instruct the farmers so that they may be able to examine what they buy. We are not restricting our efforts to educate the farmers but on the contrary are increasing them.

Are the provisions in clause 7 intended to apply to seed sold for export ? There are many noxious weeds which thrive in a climate such as ours, but might not mature in Great Britain, France or Germany, and seeds containing the seeds of such weeds might not be prejudiced thereby to anything like the same extent in those countries as in Canada. Will the provisions of this Bill apply to such seeds when sold for export ? The bulk of the seed trade in Ontario is with foreign countries, and it is not desirable that we should in any way restrict those markets.

Section G provides that no person shall sell or offer or have in his possession for sale for the purpose of seeding in Canada-Any seeds of timothy, &c.
I do not think that this restriction is in any of the other sections, but I might say that, as a matter of fact, our seed merchants export almost entirely the highest quality of seed. That is one of the evils we have to contend with, namely, that the best quality is exported and the inferior sold in Canada. The best quality is exported to countries where they have just such legislation as

we are now proposing. Consequently these countries have been able to get better seeds than our own farmers can procure. The Bill applies to all seeds held for sale in Canada, whether intended for export or not. If it did not, we would be constantly hampered in the enforcement of the law by having to decide whether the seed was intended or not for export.

What the hon. minister says may be true as regards European markets, but the United States are prepared to buy all grades of seeds. They will not pay the same prices, but will buy any seeds at* a price. It appears to me important that this Bill should only apply to seeds sold retail for use in Canada. Why should we lessen the value of goods which we send to a foreign country ? If you will prevent dealers from buying certain seed even for export, you will make a marketable commodity a dead stock in the hands of the growers or merchants. I do not think this Bill should apply to seeds intended for export. We can safely let the foreign countries look after their own interests.

I have no desire to protect foreign countries, but the difficulty of carrying out this measure would be very much greater if -we were to allow seed to be held in this country, ostensibly for export. of a quality inferior to what is allowed to be sold in the country.

I do not agree with the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt). We should apply to seed for export the same test as to seed for use in the country. We should endeavour to gain the reputation of growing the best seed in the world, just as the growers in Germany of the sugar beet seed are reputed to grow seed that cannot be excelled. France has a similar reputation for cauliflower seed. When you want the best cauliflower seed, you must go to France. One word with reference to the fear expressed that this trade will go into the hands of a very few. As a matter of fact, the wholesale trade is limited to a very few and that is a good thing. How does this particular trade work' A wholesale firm sends out a traveller to the retail dealers in Renfrew. He tells these dealers that if he can sell a sufficient quantity to send a carload to the town of Renfrew, whence it could be distributed to the various other places, he will do it on more favourable terms. The freight is a very important factor. If the retailer can buy at wholesale prices every kind of seed he* wants and have it delivered cheaply at his own door, he will not fail to do so because he would then be able to undersell everybody else in his own vicinity.

If the Bill should pass in its present shape, it may lead to some confusion. and some guiltless persons may possibly suffer. The main object of the Bill is to protect the farmer who desires to keep his farm clean and to purchase seed free from noxious weeds. I would suggest that in every case the purchaser should be entitled to a certificate from the seller to the effect that the seller has sold a certain quantity of a certain seed to the purchaser for seed purposes and has sold it, knowing that he is incurring all the responsibility under this Act. We should provide further that any seed sold without such certificate shall be deemed to have been sold for other than seeding purposes. That would meet the many objections raised. The objection that this Bill would drive the trade into the hands of the large dealers does not apply. As a fact the majority of seed merchants purchase their seeds from the wholesale seed merchants who have the appliances for cleaning.
Again, if we say that, in order that the farmer may be protected by the provision of the Bill, the seed merchant in the country store will suffer, then, I say, so let it be; it is a case of the greatest good to the greatest number. We might apply the same argument and say :	We will allow every
person to sell drugs : We will allow every person to practice medicine. But we do not apply the argument in that way. There is another thing that, in my opinion, might be provided for by the Act and is not. I have known many cases of farmers purchasing in the spring what they believed to be turnip seed, but what they found out too late to be rape seed. It seems to me that where that is done there must have been not merely negligence but deliberate fraud.
If there is any way of punishing the man who is guilty of selling for turnip seed something that is utterly worthless for the purpose for which it is purchased, it would be well, I think, to cover the case in this Bill. There is another point which may not properly come under this Bill as it is at present, but which could easily be allowed for by some little change in the title and might be provided for in a special section.
I would suggest that there should be a provision in the Bill that the man owning or having under his control a threshing machine should be obliged, before he leaves the premises of one farmer to go to those of another, to thoroughly clean his separator.

I sympathize very much with the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) in many of the points he has raised.
1 may tell him frankly, that, in consequence of the opposition to the details of the Bill,
I have thought it best to take one step at a time. I hope the day will come, and not very long hence, when we shall be able to go further than is provided for in this Bill, but I suppose it will be impossible, at one fell swoop to effect all the reforms in the seed trade that we would like to see, parti-_ - cularly as that trade has existed hitherto'

without control or supervision. I hope that, in the future, provisions shall be made, such as my hon. friend speaks of, but at present, I fear, we can hardly go as far as he would like. As to his first suggestion concerning a certificate accompanying every sale of seed, under the provisions of the Act, there is a subclause in section 3 providing that a certificate can be given that the provisions of the Act do not apply, but, in every other respect all the processes of the Act shall apply to every sale without a certificate required or given.
Is any law similar to tliis in force in any country so far as the minister knows, and if so, does it work well ?

I cannot say that exactly similar provisions are in force in any country that 1 know of. In certain European countries including Austria-Hungary and Switzerland, they had a system called a guarantee system which is provided for by law and which seems to work fairly well. But I hardly thought the condition of the trade here such that we could safely introduce that system. I have taken most of the provisions of this law from laws somewhat similar in their nature-but dealing with other subjects-already in force in Canada. I have taken some of the provisions from the Fruit Marks Act, and of the General Inspection Act.
I understood that they had a law on this subject in Germany and also in Great Britain, and I wondered how they compared with this and whether they were successful or not.

There are laws on this subject in European countries much more drastic than this. When I first drew this Bill, a couple of years ago, I was much closer to those models than I am in the Bill as now presented. I have been modifying in the direction of leniency, and as I said to my hon. friend (Mr. Miller), I think that it is necessary to proceed a step at a time.
I trust that with the improvement in the trade which, I am sure, will result from the passage of this law, we shall be able to go further as the trade can stand it.
On section 8,
I would like to ask the minister if it is the intention that a person shall be punishable only when he has violated the provisions of sections of 3, 4 and 5-all of them ? That is the way it is drawn.

I do not think my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonell) has read the section. It says :
Every person who, by himself or through the agency of another person violates any of the provisions of sections 3, 4 and 5

*
He is punishable if he violates any of the provisions. There is a misprint in my copy of the Act which 1 should like to correct. :I move that in line 3 or of section 8, the figure 5 be struck out and the figure 6 substituted. Section 5 is not a provision of the Act that can be violated, though section G is

Amendment agreed to.
Mr. macdonell. i would stni urge upon the minister the point that the person should be liable if he violated any one of the previous sections-3, 4 or 5. The Act, as drawn, makes these sections cumulative, it brackets the three of them, and says that a man must offend against the provisions of all three sections in order to be liable to indictment. If he offends against any one section, it should be sufficient. 1 submit the matter as a legal question, and the word ' or ' should be substituted for the word ' and.'

I am not prepared to set up my own opinion against the legal opinion of my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonell), who is a lawyer of high standing. But I do not read it in that way, and I would be disposed to risk the enforcement of the Act with the words as they are in the section.

The line seems to be rather heavy. I understand that these costs may be levied upon every package. That is unnecessarily severe. If it is pointed out to him that one of these packages is wrong and he can fall back on the parties from whom he got it, why, of course, he will do it. But to fine him on the whole fifty7 packages when he is only selling from one seems to be rather severe. Further, I cannot ascertain where the responsibility of the retailer begins and the responsibility of the wholesaler ends. I do not find in this clause a point at which it may be said that the wholesaler is relieved and the retailer becomes responsible. And when the retailer becomes responsible, it does not appear that he is ever relieved so long as the result of that crop is unknown. I would ask whether he is relieved before or after the crop has been reaped ? If it is open for a man to come back six months afterwards and say: That seed II got from you is not pure seed- of which there is no evidence that he did get it, he only says so-there is a great diliiculty7. Now, as a dealer, I might buy in the early part of the season from a man in Toronto, later in the season I would buy7, say7, from a man in Hamilton, and I might also buy from Chicago. It would be impossible for me to tell which of these three lots I sold from to an individual who might complain at the end of the season. Therefore, the responsibility rests upon the seller, and it is not clear where it begins and where it ends.
In the first place, in a case where there is no proof. I do not think thef

person accused would have very much to fear, because without proof he cannot be condemned. In the second place, in regard to the retailer and the wholesaler, the case would be In regard to a certain sale, whoever made that sale would be responsible. The provisions of subsections 2 and 3 of this section enable a person who has made a sale to escape responsibility of that sale under certain conditions which are here detailed, one of which is that it was a seed package the seal of which had not been broken. The other is that he must prove to the satisfaction of the court that he had not tampered with the seed, and that it was really in the condition in which he obtained it, and that he had sold it in good faith. He would have to prove this to relieve himself from responsibility. The proof on which he would be relieved of responsibility would no doubt serve in a court of law against the person who sold it to him. 'So far as the protection of the wholesaler who sells to the retailer is concerned, the wholesaler would have no responsibility if the retailer sold again, because the last purchase would be the only purchase on which a case could be founded, unless under the circumstances to which I have just referred. The hon. gentleman also spoke about a minimum penalty, that is to say, that if a person sold a large number of packages he might be unfairly mulcted in a considerable sum.
Now, if my hon. friend will study the section carefully, he will see that while there is a maximum limit there is no minimum limit. In the amount to be imposed on him for each package, the magistrate or the court, I suppose, who imposed the fine would take all the circumstances into consideration. If he judged that a small amount would suffice to punish him and to indicate that he had done wrong, the amount placed on the sale of each individual package would be so nominal that the whole amount he would have to pay would be very small.

Suppose a farmer purchases from a retailer and he finds tluft the seed is not good and proceeds against the retailer. But the retailer gets out of it on the ground that he purchased the seed from a wholesale dealer or some other person ; then would the farmer have to proceed against the wholesale dealer ?

I think subsection 3 of this Act would meet such circumstances :
Every magistrate who has disposed of any case under 'the foregoing subsection shall, within one month from the date of his judgment therein, send to the Minister of Agriculture a report of the case.
I think it will then be the duty of the department to take up the case and proceed. Although that is not expressly stated, I think it is implied that such a case as the hon. gentleman indicates would be one that the department might properly take up.
Is that the object for which a report is to be made ?
Yes.

I think the minister would be assuming a grave duty in deciding whether he should take it up or not. This section makes it optional for the Depart-msnt of Agriculture to interfere in the case.
I may say that I think the intention of the minister in drawing this Bill is a good one. But I regret that we have not sufficient information before us as to how similar Acts work in other countries to enable us to judge of the probable effect of this one. I think we should proceed very slowly on such information as we can get. I think the committee ought to be placed in possession of an abstract of the legislation passed in other countries on this subject, that would enable us to come to a conclusion as to whether we should pass this measure in its present form or not. If there is a law on the statutes of the United States, as I think the Minister of Agriculture said there was, we ought to be placed* iu possession of it. 'I think the Bill will largely increase the price of seeds to farmers, and I think that a large majority of farmers, after purchasing their seeds, will hesitate very much before going into court and taking the chance of getting a remedy for the sale of impure seeds to them.

I think my hon. friend (Mr. A. Martin) does not quite give the farmers the credit which is due them for defending themselves. We have a number of laws on the statute-book to protect trade in various ways. We have the General Inspection Act, we have the Act which deals with commercial fertilizers and a number of other Acts, all of which are framed for the purpose of protecting the individual in his trade. This is anoher Act of the same character. The point my hon. friend brought out in regard to the government, or the department, proceeding and taking up cases is one in regard to which I do not agree with him. 1 do not think it ought to he imperative under the Act, because circumstances vary so much that it would be necessarily left in the discretion of the minister of the department as to what should be proceeded with and as to what should not be proceeded with. That is the invariable rule in all cases that come under the Inspection Acts, and in this case I think it would be absolutely necessary as in the other cases.

I think it would not be a good feature of the Bill that it should be left in the hands of the Department of Agriculture to determine whether the purchaser shall have any remedy or not. It might lead to some very improper decisions by the Minister of Agriculture and some farmers might suffer while some others might get the benefit. Information in reference to the working of similar enact-



meats in other countries is wanting. The hon. minister did not enlighten the committee in this respect. It is very well to protect the farmers, but I am afraid this is a Bill for the lawyers to fight over. I would gladly support an effective and workable Bill, but this one is full of difficulties. The committee should have better information in reference to what has been done in other and older countries.

Under any circumstances and in any case the department or any in-jdividual could proceed. It is an offence against the law. The Bill does not limit the prosecution to the person who suffers.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
