Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
What is the object of the 3rd subsection of section 8 ?

The object of the third subsection of section 8 is to provide in case the person accused of selling fraudulently has proved that he was not himself responsible for the condition of the seeds, then an approach may be made to the Minister of Agriculture so that if it is thought necessary or advisable, departmental action can be taken for the carrying on of the prosecution. If my kon. friend will read the section just preceding he will see under what conditions and circumstances the seller can clear himself of a charge of breach of the Act. When he has done so some one else is evidently guilty and section 3 provides that the department may be notified of the condition of affairs, may take it into consideration and if it is thought advisable may institute a prosecution against the party who is guilty.
Not against this person.
No, against the person who is guilty.
They may commence a new prosecution.

Would the Minister of Agriculture explain to us what would be done in a case where a retail merchant had bought seed in rui unbroken package, had sold it and it was subsequently found that the seed had originally been supplied to the retail merchant from a wholesale merchant in a foreign country. How could the man be punished ?
We could not do anything.

In this case the retailer is summoned and brought before the court by the farmer, but when the retailer proves that he is innocent but that the wholesaler from whom he has bought the Mr. A. MARTIN.
seed is the guilty person what does the minister propose to do ? He proposes that the retailer who is innocent shall pay the costs, and what remedy has the retailer'? He has only to transmit that evidence to the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Agriculture may pigeon-hole the complaint after subjecting him to costs. In my opinion this is a Bill altogether in the interests of the wholesale dealers. When an action such as this section provides is brought against a retailer an opportunity should be given to him to proceed against the wholesaler without having to submit to the Department of Agriculture the question of whether or not he should be able to do so. Favouritism might be shown in such a case. The department might take action in the case of a retailer who is friendly to them and do nothing in the case of a retailer who was not. If the retailer is to be subjected to costs he should have an opportunity of proceeding against the wholesaler from whom he has bought.
If my hon. friend reads the Act he will see there is nothing in it to prevent that either.

The section reads :
Nevertheless, if the accused proves to the magistrate before whom he is tried that' the package, sack, bag or receptacle containing the seed respecting which the complaint or information is laid, was purchased by him directly from a seed merchant domiciled in Canada, and was not opened, or the state of the seed was not altered, while it was in his possession, and he had no reason to believe that the seed did not comply with the provisions of this Act, he shall, upon disclosing the name of the person from whom he purchased the seed, and the place and date of the sale thereof, to him, not be liable beyond the costs of prosecution.
What is the next step ? Is there a provision here that the retailer shall fall back on the wholesaler ? No. It says :
Every magistrate who has disposed of any case under the foregoing subsection shall, within one mohth from the date of his judgment therein, send to the Minister of Agriculture a report of the case, giving the name of the accused, the name of -the- person who sold the seed to him, and the date and place of such sale.
That is all he has to do, and it is then for the Minister of Agriculture to say what is to be done. He may say : Well this man is obnoxious to us, he has mulcted him in costs, but there is no remedy for him. An-ctker person may he viewed with more friendly eyes by the Minister of Agriculture, who will say we will pi'oceed in this case and bring the wholesaler into court. I do not think that this power should be placed in the hands of the Minister of Agriculture or any other minister.

My hon. friend has read the conclusive proof of what I just told him ; there is nothing in this Act to prevent the retailer himself proceeding against the

person who sold the goods. The magistrate is obliged to report the case to the Minister of Agriculture in case the minister should think it is a case in which proceedings should be taken, whether the retailer cares to do so or not. But the retailer has all the machinery of this Act to protect himself. There is nothing in the Act to prevent him from proceeding against the wholesaler.

There is nothing in the Act and that is the whole trouble. In place of allowing the farmer to have a judgment against the retailer and the retailer to fall 'back on the wholesaler as it should be in the Bill.

It is so in the Bill. That is what this subsection means. I have informed tbe hon. gentleman and the House that it means that the magistrate shall report the case to the minister in case the minister thinks it necessary to proceed, but that does not debar the retailer from proceeding against the wholesaler. The retailer has at his disposal the whole machinery of the Act just as the farmer had against the retailer. I have stated that to the hon. gentleman and I cannot make it any clearer.

Well, I cannot make it very much clearer to the hon. minister. What my contention is, is this, that when the farmer brings a suit against the retailer, and the seed is proved to be faulty, he should be able to get a judgment against the retailer ; and if the retailer is aggrieved, let him get his remedy from the wholesaler.
I think that would be a great improvement on the Bill.
I think it would be unfair to the retailer, if he is able to supply the proof described in subsection 2, to have a judgment rendered against him, and I want to protect the retailer to that extent.

The Minister of Agriculture knows very well that the farmers of this country are not going to law against the wholesaler in Montreal or Toronto. Take the ease of a farmer in Prince Edward Island, who buys seed from a retail merchant and brings him into court and proves that the seed was not what it was represented to be. He cannot get judgment against the retailer because the retailer falls back on the wholesaler in Toronto. The Minister of Agriculture expects the farmer to proceed against the wholesaler
No.
Or leave it to the Department of Agriculture.

That would be a case in which it would be quite proper for the minister to take up the case and proceed against the wholesaler ; but at the same time there is nothing to debar the retailer 121
in Prince Edward Island from proceeding against the wholesaler himself.

It is a great objection, I think, to this Bill that the farmer, after bringing the suit against the retailer and proving his case, should then be compelled to go against the -wholesaler in a distant part of Canada.

I ask the minister to explain clause 8. It is said that the fine need not exceed $5 for the first offence. It can therefore be up to $5, and that fine shall be in respect of each receptacle, package, sack or bag, and it may apply to a case where a man has it in his possession for sale, contrary to the said provision. I want the minister to say to the committee whether that will cover a case of this kind. A dealer gets a large quantity in bulk of any kind of seed and does it up into a thousand packages. Then it is discovered that he has that seed for sale, and that it has this improper admixture of noxious weeds in it. Is it contemplated by the minister that an information may be laid charging this man with having a thousand packages of a certain kind of seed for sale contrary to the provisions of the Act, and that he may be fined in respect of each of these packages to the extent of $5, so that there could be inflicted by a magistrate-a magistrate who has, perhaps, no great knowledge of law-a fine of $5,000, or in default of payment a term of one month's imprisonment.
Mr. FISHER, Yes, under the reading of the Act the extraordinary case which my hon. friend cites might occur ; but I would trust to common sense and judgment of a magistrate to deal with the case on its merits, and to put the fine on each individual package low enough not to make it such an outrageous and extraordinary fine. Were such a fine as my hon friend speaks of inflicted, I think it would be a proper case to take on appeal to a higher court ; so that the last resort would not be left in the hands of what my horn friend has described as an ignorant country magistrate.
I do not propose to take the language of the hon. minister. I did not use the term * ignorant country magistrate.' The minister may have very good reasons for wishing to put it in that form.
No, I thought that was what the hon. gentleman said.
Allow me to say that the hon. minister is mistaken.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon.

I said that it might be dealt w>th by a magistrate who had no great knowledge of law. I suppose that might happen with a magistrate, as it might with a Minister of the Crown. I submit to those

in this House who have a knowledge of law that the hon. minister is not right in suggesting that in the case it put there could not be a successful appeal to a higher court. There would not be ground for an appeal. The magistrate would not have gone beyond the limits of the evidence and would not have exceeded his jurisdiction. If there 'S any such rule of law as that a judgment of a magistrate can he set aside when he acts within the limits laid down by the statute, it would be important to this House to be acquainted with that fact. As I understand it, there is no such rule of law. The case I put is clear, and I believe it is beyond question. It is not beyond the imagination of members of this House that there might be times when it would be very satisfactory to a magistrate to impose just such a fine, and it might happen that in the next adjoining municipality a person would be fined simply $5 or less for a single offence. There is liable to be great inequality and a great perversion of justice under this section. I do not say it with any desire to carp particularly about the Act, but I think it is well worth while for the minister, who,
.1 will imagine, is anxious to advance the interests of the farming class, to consider whether that would be a wise provision.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As the hon. gentleman says, it is quite true that inconvenience would result from the application of the law as stated here ; but the hon. gentleman is aware that cumulative penalties are not at all unknown to the profession. They have arisen under the Banking Act and under the Railway Act. I have a case in mind of a bank having been proceeded against for an enormous amount by cumulative penalty. How does my hon. friend propose to deal with a matter of this kind ? My attention has frequently been drawn to this difficulty, and up to the present time I have not found a remedy. If my hon. friend could suggest a remedy, I have no doubt the Minister of Agriculture would be glad to apply it.
You might make a maximum aggregate fine.-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The fine is 55 for each particular offence. If a man sells one package, the fine of $5 would not be excessive, and if he sells one hundred, the principle is the same-he has committed one hundred offences.
He may have made only one sale, and yet have a thousand packages for sale.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite right. What has been pointed out is a serious inconvenience ; the point is to find some remedy. It might not only be an inconvenience but something more. It might be an injustice.
My hon. friend the Minister of Justice has met this matter in the spirit I expected. It is not the case of a second offence

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is for cumulative offences.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I quite appreciate the point and the remark made by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. But there is this difficulty. You must not deal with a large offender on more favourable terms than with a small offender. The discussion has been profitable. I do not think that this Bill can leave the committee tonight, and I would like to deal with the point now made in such a way as not to create an unfortunate precedent.
A person who had a thousand packages might not be a large dealer. A very small quantity might be divided into a thousand packages.

I think the position taken by the Minister of Justice is very reasonable. But whichever way you have it, you will have some inconvenience. It would be a great hardship to have this cumulative penalty- put upon a dealer who really was not very guilty after all, and you might sometimes fail to mete out proper punishment to an inveterate breaker of the law. We might, however, take the more lenient course, and limit the maximum penalty ; and then if we found that the law did not work well, we could change it.

I am quite willing to let that section stand in order that I may look into the matter with my colleague. We thought that by making no limit to the smallness of the penalty, we were giving the opportunity for the imposition of a very light sentence, even when a large number of packages was concerned.
Section 8 is allowed to stand.
On section 9-who shall be prima facie liable.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This is to prevent the penalty being imposed on the clerk.
On section 10-examination of seeds, payment of samples, penalty for preventing examination.
Is it the intention to appoint an inspector ?
Wre shall require a staff for the purpose of enforcing the Act.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: This is the object-to give employment to a staff of hungry officials.

The hon. gentleman makes a statement quite unwarranted, not in accord with the facts, and for which he has no foundation. The object of the Bill has *been explained, my hon. friend knows it well, and he deliberately undertakes to misrepresent it.
I rise to a point of order. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, whether it is in order for any member to say that another deliberately misrepresents the object of a Bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister probably went a little too far in using the term 1 deliberately,' but was no doubt provoked to use the term by the hon. member for Leeds who imputed an unworthy motive to the hon. minister, and was equally out of order.
You are most accommodating, Mr. Chairman. On being called to give a decision upon one point of order, you take up another, and we are very much obliged for the double ruling.

I think the committee should have some information from the Minister as to the number of persons who are to be employed in carrying out this Act, what their duties will be and about how much the cost to the country will amount to.
So far as I can see at present, there will be no necessary additions to the staff I now have.
Then, the hon. minister must have too many now.
The minister spoke of analysts-these, I suppose, he already has in the department ?
Yes.

Section 10 authorizes ' any person charged with the enforcement of this Act ' to enter premises under certain circumstances. That would seem to indicate that persons are to be appointed to enforce the Act; and it seems to me that if the Act is to be made efficient, the minister must employ people to enforce it. As my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Martin) suggests, this is a good time for the minister to take the committee into his confidence and tell us what the cost of enforcing the law will be, as measured by the salaries of the officials who will be necessary.
For education and analytical work, I already 'have a staff

A staff distributed over the country ?
Mr. FISHER, They travel part of the time carrying on educational and organization work, and part of the time they are in the office at Ottawa. There are four or five men under the head of this branch, Mr. Clark. I hope to utilize the services of these men where it is necessary for the department to intervene. They now collect specimens-where we do not get them voluntarily sent in-by purchasing in the open market. That kind of work has been going on for four years. It may be necessary to add one or two to that staff, not so much with a view to enforcing this Act, but to assist in the general work of the department, and, as part of that work, to supervise the enforcement of the Act. I think it will generally be enforced by those who are defrauded and who take advantage of the Act as a means of protecting themselves. In cases such as those covered by section 8, the department might intervene through one of its officials, whose duty it would be to put a case in the hands of the Department of Justice. And we shall be able, when we think it necessary, to employ the Dominion Police to enforce this law, the same as any law, in cases where the government finds it necessary to intervene. At present I have no intention of adding to the staff in the way of inspectors to go about the country and specially do the work of enforcing the law.
What would be the position of a purchaser of seeds who found the field in which the seed had been sown grown up with weeds, though he had not noticed the weed-seeds before sowing ?

He would be competent to proceed under the Act, but the difficulties of proof would be very great, unless he had taken the precaution to take a sample of the seed under the provisions of the Act soon after purchasing the seed. But auy farmer, knowing the Act to be in force, if he had any suspicion of the seed he had

bought, would take a sample, and then he would be armed for procedure if he found it necessary to act.
I am inclined to think the seedsman would order him out of his place of business if he tried to take a sample, because it would be throwing suspicion on the goods.
The seller need not know anything about his taking a sample under the Act.
I thought the sample had to be taken in the place where the seed was bought.
Yes; or in the presence of two disinterested witnesses.
Pie could buy it, take it home and sample it there 1
He would have to prove that it was the seed that he had got from the individual.

In our section we grow a great deal of alsike. Some of it is exported to be used, as I understand, for colouring purposes. I have had as many as twenty bags of alsike seed in the barn at apce, but I could not say, when raising the seed, what it was to be used for. Yet, under this law, as I understand it, these inspectors could come in and take samples and put me to a lot of trouble.
Wherever the person engaged in enforcing the law has reason to suppose that seeds are kept contrary to the provisions of the Act, he would have a right to enter and make an examination.

I would like to ask if there is no limit to the applications for samples ? Is the dealer obliged to furnish samples to every inspector and complainant who may demand it of him ? If they are allowed to come in and demand interminable samples, the Seedsmen will be much hampered, because the seed business is a rush trade, as every one knows. Further, I understand the minister to say that it is not necessary that the seller of the seed should be present when the sample is taken, or have any knowledge of it.- I would object to that. That was done in our town in one case and did serious harm to the dealer. Surely, the man who furnishes the sample should know what it is for. He should be able to keep a sample for liis own use, the same as he would of food products that are analyzed by the department. When the government analyst buys a pound of coffee or other article for examination, he always leaves a portion of it with the dealer, so that the latter can get it examined by another analyst if he desires. If these seeds can be taken without the knowledge or consent of the owner, I think you are doing a grievous Mr. FISHER.
i harm to the tradesman or grower behind ! his back.

With regard to the idea that any one may go in and take samples, it is to be remembered that this section only gives authority to do so to the official who is charged with the enforcement of the Act. The department is not going to instruct a dozen officials to go and take samples of any individual's crop. An ordinary informer cannot take a sample under this provision, it is only the person charged with the enforcement of this Act that is allowed to enter on a man's premises by authority and take a sample, and clause 10 says he shall not be impeded in the exercise of his authority and his duties for that purpose.

I asked about the case of a farmer who was raising alsike clover seed for export. Now I have had many bags of seed on my place at the same time, and under this clause I should think that a party would have power to come into my barn and inspect those bags whether I was willing or not, even though he might not know whether they -were going to be sold for seed or not. That would be a great hardship, and should not be allowed unless the official was notified that they were there for sale for seed. This clause allows an inspector to do that sort of thing.

No doubt the man charged with the enforcement of the Act would have such power, and if the seed is likely to be sold for seeding purposes I think a government official should have that power, as he has in many other cases. He is a government inspector for that purpose, and is empowered to enter into premises where he believes any article is being held for seed purposes contrary to law. He will have that power under this Act. I would not like to say that we should restrict that power of a government official in the exercise of his functions.

But that seems to be an extraordinary power. I do not think an official should have that power in reference to all seeds in respect to which no accusation or charge has been made. But my hon. friend here is simply the possessor of a lot of grain that he has raised and stored in his bam or 'his granary. There is no question about selling the seed for seed purposes or anything of the kind ; and without his being charged with any impropriety, you say that a certain official may enter his premises whenever he chooses and make an inspection of his grain, and if he is impeded by the owner the latter renders himself liable to a line of $500. It seems to me that is going too far, and that before your enforcer of the law can enter any premises it must ue premises in which it is supposed that there is seed out of which sales have been made for seed purposes. But this clause goes much further. Any granary, chamber, receptacle of
A

any kind in any part of the country whose owner is not selling seeds for seed purposes or anything of the kind, may be opened ar- i bitrarily by this official, and if the owner, bvho has a right in his own possession, obstructs the official he renders himself liable under the law. I think that should only take place where there is a seed about which there is a question of illegal selling for seed purposes.
This clause is exactly similar to the clause in the General Inspection Act, in the Inland Revenue Act and also in the Customs Act. Customs officers have far greater powers than are given here.

I do not think the case here is at all parallel to a case under the Customs or Inland Revenue Acts, because in these latter cases a man is defrauding the revenue.
I am not defrauding anybody, so far as I am concerned. I raise that grain myself. I am not responsible under this Act for what I do with it. I am not liable for what I do with alsike clover or anything else I have in my possession. Yet an official of the government can come into my premises whenever he sees fit and inspect my wheat; he can take a sample of wheat, or timothy with foul seed in it, as there very often is, and it is nobody's business so long as I keep it in my granary and do not sell. I do not think any government official should be allowed to come on my premises and inspect my grain when he don't know whether I have it for sale for seed or not. It is none of his business what I have it there for, unless I let the public know that I have this seed there for sale for sowing purposes.
* Mr. FISHER. There is a good deal in what the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane) says, and I think it might be well possibly to limit the application of this section in some cases. As I said before, it is taken almost verbatim from the General Inspection Act ; but the circumstances are a little different.

I would ask the minister to consider another phase of this matter. There is a penalty of $500, no for having seed that is improperly labelled, but for, in any degree, obstructing the officials. It might work out in this way : A farmer has only enough wheat upon his place to seed his own farm and feeling it to be a serious injustice that this official should come in, inspect his grain and takes a sample of it. He does, to some slight extent, obstruct the official. He has no knowledge of the law. Of course, it is said, that a want of knowledge of the law is no excuse-that every man is bound to know the law, but still we must look at this thing from a practical standpoint. He has no knowledge of the law, he knows he is right, he obstructs tuis official and he is fined. He has only enough seed to seed his farm, he has no intention of selling any, he can prove beyond question
that he had not anything to sell, he feels if an injustice that this man can come in and invade his rights and property, he obstructs him to some extent and although it is proven in the end that the grain was not offered for sale he is fined $500. I would like the hon. minister to consider that point.
Mr. FIiSlHER. The qualification which I have just suggested might be put in in accordance with the request of the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane). That will cover the point that the hon. gentleman speaks of.
Very good.

In regard to that other question it seems to me it is not very clear yet, that is, as to who may take samples of seed, and under what circumstances they may be taken for the government analyst. The Bill says ' any inspector, informant or complainant.'
That is the 11th clause.

Yes, my first question was : must these samples be taken in the presence of the person who sold the seed ? And the hon. minister's first reply was that this was quite unnecessary. I see there is a provision which says :
Any inspector, informant' or complainant who, finds or suspects seeds to be sold, or offered, exposed or had in possession for sale for the purpose of seeding in violation of the provisions of this Act, shall take a sample from the said seeds and forward it to such person as the Governor in Council appoints as an official seed analyst to examine and report upon any seed submitted for analysis under the provisions of this Act.
Section 12 provides that:
Any sample of seed taken for official analysis

This may be taken by either the inspector, informant or complainant :

under the provisions of this Act shall be
taken in the presence of-
(a)	the person who sold or offered, exposed or had in his possession for sale the said seeds, or
(b)	two impartial or non-interested witnesses.
Would it be competent for a person when purchasing seed to take it home, then afterwards call in two impartial witnesses, take a sample of the seed and send it to the government analyst ?

Yes. The farmer who purchases the seed need not necessarily take a sample in the store before he leaves. He may take it home. He may send his servant or his boy to buy the seed and when he gets this seed home, according to the provisions of section 13, he may take a sample ' within seven days from the date on which the seeds entered into the personal possession and became the property of the puchas-er.' It would never do to restrict the tak-

ing of a sample of the seeds to the moment of purchasing the seeds. We -would practically nullify the operation of the Act. Of course, when the sample is taken it has to be taken fairly in the presence of two unbiased, unprejudiced: witnesses who will certify to its being a fair sample of the seeds.
Mr. iSPROULE. This applies to seeds that are not sold in sealed packages. Suppose seeds are sold in sealed packages, wha't then ?

There are two cases provided under section 13. One is the case where seed is sold in a sealed package. I am glad to know that a number of the best seedsmen are putting up their seeds in small sealed packages for the express purpose of protecting their own reputation, and the seed is sold through the retailer in an unbroken package bearing the seedsman's seal. Then, a sample must be taken at the time of breaking the seedsman's seal. Where the seed is sold in bulk and then retailed, we have to make other provisions and the provisions are as contained in section 13. Samples are to be taken within seven days and under section 12 they must be taken in the presence of two impartial and non-interested witnesses. I think we safeguard the seller as well as we possibly can.

In reference to section 11, second line, does not the hon. minister think that is a little loose ?
Any inspector, informant or complainant' who finds or suspects seeds to be sold, &c.
Any man of a suspicious turn of mind is always suspecting things. We quite well know what little rivalries and jealousies are likely to take place.
That is only as regards the taking of the sample. If he did not suspect he would not take the sample at all. We must allow him to take the sample on suspicion.
What does my hon. friend want him to have ?
He should have some good ground for believing. He should have some prima facie evidence. Any man ean suspect anything, and suspicious men are apt to suspect anything.
You cannot get the evidence until you have taken a sample and analysed it.
Neither could a man enter a house and take a criminal from that house until he had some basis for doing so.
It is not a question of going into a man's house. It is simply the taking of a sample.
It is a question of interfering with a man's property. He should have some reasonable ground for believing.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Inland Revenue).
speechtext: I may say that in regard to the Adulteration Act It is almost similar to this provision of the Bill. Where there is ground for suspecting that the law has been violated the inspector may go into a house and get samples; in fact, we generally give instructions to the inspectors to go into every store where they think goods are being offered for sale which do not comply with the law and procure samples. I suppose the same principle might apply in this case, 'there is nothing injurious to any person in the fact that collections of samples are made.
But you do that for the safety of the public health.
Do I understand that when taking these samples they are obliged to pay for them ?
Yes.
Under section 10, but not under section 11.

Section 11 provides for the taking of a sample from what the purchaser has. It is not a forcible entry and the taking of a sample from somebody else's seed. It is the taking of a sample from the seed which has been purchased and which is in the possession of the purchaser who must take it and forward the seed to the analyst.
Is that correct ?
I understand so.

I am not quite sure of that. It you take section 11 and section 12 together I think that section 12 will probably embrace what is provided for in section 11, and section 11 authorizes an inspector, informant or complainant who finds or suspects seeds, &c., to take a sample from the said seeds and forward it to the government analysts, and then any sample of seeds taken shall be taken in a certain way according to section 12. Do not these two sections go together ?
Certainly.

But then the inspector, informant or complainant can go into the premises of a person who has not sold one bushel or one package of grain and take a sample and not pay for it, whereas under section 10 if you take samples you must pay for them. I cannot see the reason for that difference.

My reading of it is that section 10 gives authority to enter in and take a sample where there is somebody objecting to the taking of a sample, for instance from a merchant's bin or dealer's bag. There the person charged with the enforcement of the Act is given certain authority and power ; similar authority and power is given under the Customs Act, the Inland Revenue Act, and the Adulteration of Foods Act. It is not an unusual power at all. It is given under most of the Acts connected with the administration of just such things as this in Canada. But to return for a moment to my point. This section 10 provides for the taking of a sample when there is objection on the part of the owner of the grain to the taking of the sample, and the person charged with the enforcement of the Act has to exercise his authority and rights in order to perform his duty. Section 10 gives him that authority and that right. Section 11 provides that in a case that is in dispute, a sample must be taken to be forwarded to the government analyst for test or analysis, and it says that, that sample shall be taken by anybody who is entering upon a prosecution or a case or even if he does not want to enter into a case, if he simply suspects he has been wrongly treated he will take a sample of the grain and forward it to the government laboratory for analysis. Section 12 provides necessary precaution as to how and under what conditions a sample is to be taken which is to be forwarded for analysis. If the sample were not taken under these conditions, the analysis of the sample could not be used as proof in a test case. That is the object of section 10, to provide regulations and conditions under which a sample should be taken, the result of analysis of which would be used in a test case. I think these are the reasons for having three different sections ; they deal with the matter in three different ways.
Section 11 can be taken with section 12.
Yes ; any samples taken under section 11 must be taken in the way prescribed in section 12.

Section 11 goes very far. It embraces any case where goods are to be sold or offered, exposed or had in possession for the purpose of sale, and so on. It embraces any case where any person has these goods for sale. Then any inspector, informant or complainant may take a sample of seed with or against the owner's will and send it to the analyst, so that I do not see exactly why, if it is to be paid for in the case my hon. friend mentioned before, it should not be paid for in this case. That this provision applies to seller as well as buyer is further borne out, I think, by the provision in section 12 that a sample may be taken in the presence of (a) :
The person who sold or offered for sale or had in his possession for sale, such seed.
Now, if this did not apply to the dealer or grower, how could the sample be taken in the presence of the person who offered, exposed or had it in his possession for sale?. These are words which show plainly that not only does it embrace the case which the minister refers to as a case where a person has suffered. and therefore voluntarily acts, and might be supposed to surrender his sample without payment, but also that it applies to the other case of the dealer or grower, and if there is good reason for having provision for payment in the 10th section, I submit to the minister that there is much more reason for having it in the case of these two sections, for this reason that in this case there are a variety of people, not alone a government official who is always doing justice, but a variety of people who may act ; we have an inspector, an informant, and a complainant, and the informants and the complainants may if they think fit be legion. A may take a sample to-day, B to-morrow, and C the next day. There is no limit to the possible number of samples, and thus a valuable seed might be frittered away by enemies. That is not a probability, but it is a possibility, and a law should be certain. The Minister of Agriculture brings in the analogy of adulterated food, Surely he does not think that there is any analogy between a case of malfeasance such as that, a deliberate act of adulterating food, and the act of an honest farmer who has in his possession grain which he has no suspicion offends against this law, grain which contains seeds of which he does not know the name and which he has no means of testing. One is a direct crime against the laws and the other is at most a mere matter of neglect or want of knowledge or nonfeasance.

Will section 11 apply to any inspector ? No one has a right to go in and take a sample contrary to the desire of the owner except the government officials. The informant or complainant cannot do it except by the permission of the person owning the seed.
You make it imperative because you say ' shall.'
That ' shall ' means that in case of taking a sample for the analyst in order to get evidence for a prosecution; a sample shall be taken which shall serve the purpose.
He may be an informant or an inspector.

I would not say that this section at all authorizes any informant or complainant or even an inspector to go into a place against the owner's will but of course I would not give a legal opinion on it. Section 10 does give that authority to the inspector.
You tell him to do that knowing that he has not the authority.
I tell him to do a thing which, for a purpose, I presume he is able to do. If he is not able to do it I suppose he must get the sample in some other way.
' Shall ' is oi'dinarily imperative. Will the minister allow these two sections to stand for consideration ?

I am perfectly willing to let them stand.
Sections 11 and 12 allowed to stand.
On section 13-Samples to be sent within seven days.

What guarantee will there be to the dealer that the seed will reach the analytic department in the same shape as when it left the retailer's hands $ That is a very important matter. Seed might be surreptitiously placed in a parcel that was purchased. I would remind the hon. minister of the parable of the tares. He will remember that according to Holy Writ, a man sowed good wheat in his fields and at night, while he slept, the enemy sowed tares, and when the seeds sprang up the owner found both growing togethei-. It might be so in this case. I would like to know what safeguard there is that the samples, when they reach the analyst, will be exactly the same as they were when they left the dealer's hands.

Under section 17 the Governor in Council may make i-egulations, and in these we pi-opose to provide for the method of despatching the samples to the seed laboratory.
On section 14-analysis and certificate.

Might I ask the Minister of Agriculture how many places in Canada will he available to anybody wishing to have seed tested ? Will it all have to be sent hei'e to Ottawa from every part of Canada ? If so, I think it will be a very sei'ious hindrance to the grain trade. Everybody acquainted with the trade knows that all the seed business is done inside of a few weeks, and every dealer buys very carefully, for the reason that he knows that if thei'e is any left over, he will have to carry it for twelve months. Perhaps half the seed sold by dealers is sold on rush oi'ders by wire to headquarters, and has to be hurried out at once. What opportunity would there be for a dealer to send samples to a central place and have them sent back before retailing the seed to his customers ? How long would it probably take, say from Manitoba, or from the maritime provinces, or from British Columbia ?

I suppose that for the present there would be only one seed laboratory for analysis in the city of Ottawa. It Mr. FISHER.
is true, as my hon. friend says, the seed business is rushed pretty strongly in the spring, and I do not think it would be possible for the retailer to wait for an analysis of the seed he is selling. On receiving the seed he would take a sample and send it for analysis, and in the meantime would probably have to go on selling the seed. However, in section 8, subsections 2 and 3, machinery is provided by which, if he were prosecuted for selling bad seeds, and he had a sample taken in the way I speak of that would be a proof that would eliable him to relieve himself of the l'esponsibility and pass it on to the wholesaler who had sold him the seeds.

Another point while
1	am on my feet. Anybody having a suspicion that any seed may he impure and not up to the requirements of this Act, should immediately send a sample to the Department of Agriculture. I think twelve months is altogether too long in order to ascertain whether action is going to be taken with regard to any seed. I think that anybody feeling aggrieved should be able to get an answer back .within three months.

That point comes up later on.
On section 15-certificate as evidence.

I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Justice to the words 'shall be accepted as evidence.' Sometimes it is provided that it shall be prima facie evidence in a matter of this kind. I presume that it shall only be accepted as evidence in the case, not as necessarily conclusive evidence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would not think it would be looked on as conclusive at all- merely as part of the evidence in the case.

I think that is fail1.
On section 18-time for prosecution limited.
Should we not better limit that to 6 months ?

It was six months in the old Act. My reason for changing it to twelve was the case contemplated in subsection
2	of section 8. In such a case, if the prosecution failed against the retail dealer, it would have to be continued against the wholesale dealer, and if the limit were made six months, there might be a failure of justice.
In that case the extension is quite right, but in ordinary cases the limit should be only six months.
I shall consider the point and perhaps we might make the limit of twelve months apply only to cases under subsection 2 of section 8.

This clause is rather vague. It says that any prosecution may be

commenced within twelve months from the time when the matter of complaint or information arose and not later. What is that time ? Is it the time of sale by the wholesale dealer or resale by the retail dealer ? There might also be a doubt as to the nature of the offence. One of the offences is the exposing for sale. A merchant might expose for sale during two years and no prosecution be taken against him within those two years. If one were taken subsequently, what would be the position ? In my opinion none could be because the twelve months from the time when the matter of complaint or information arose would be up. It seems to me the clause might be made clearer.
This clause was taken verbatim from the Summary Convictions Act. The clause in that Act is well understood and its interpretation well established by the courts.

I am not aware of any provision in the Summary Convictions Act which makes the exposing for sale an offence. Supposing a man had the goods exposed for sale a couple of years, what date would you take as that on which the matter of complaint or information arose '!
I cannot answer the legal question my hon. friend has raised. I submitted the matter to the Department of Justice and they evidently considered that this clause covered the case.

Suppose information is not laid for six months or a year and no report given on the sample and the seedsman in the meantime goes on selling, how is the farmer to be protected ?
_ Mr. FISHER. I hope there will not be 'any such delay in analysing the samples and giving a report. The report should be given in two or three months at the longest. But this Bill is intended to act rather as a deterrent than as a means of punishment. Merchants will be very careful, because if they are fined a few times, they will get a reputation for selling bad seed and lose their trade. In that way the Act will do more good perhaps than by punishing wrong transactions.
On section 2 :
This Act shall come into operation on the first day of September, 1905.

I think the delay is not sufficient. A great deal of seed will be on hand at that period, timothy seed just begins to sell freely in Ontario at that date. Fall wheat is then sown from the seed of the former season and the new seed is not on the market in time for the sowing of the fall wheat. There ought to be more time given the dealers, who have large amounts of seeds that may be condemned, to get rid of their stock on hand either by exporting it or cleaning it or in some other
way. A vast amount of stuff is held by the seedsmen from one season to another, and to bring in a sweeping Act which would take away thousands of dollars worth of property from the seedsman, as this will, is not in accord with justice. I think the time should be extended six months or a year.

,1 do not take much account of the idea that this Act will come into force too soon. Everybody in Canada has been fully warned that it is coming into force. The trade expected it last year, but unfortunately the pressure of business prevented its becoming law. I have been informed by those who are more expert than I in trade matters that any time between June 15 and September 15 would be the most convenient to the trade for the changed conditions, and have therefore made the date September
1.	There can be no doubt that the Senate will pass the measure, and the trade will have six months in which to prepare for it. I am quite prepared to consider -any date for the coming season which would be most convenient to the trade, but do not think we should put it off for another season.
The time of the year that the hon. gentleman has selected is the proper one-between June and September. But I think that 1906 would be a better date to bring in so sweeping a measure.
They have had warning.

There is a vast quantity of seed in the hands of dealers that would not pass under the Act, and to make a law under which that property, perhaps, cannot be realized on at all, will be a very serious loss to individuals. It may reflect upon our farmers as well, who hold over considerable quantities.
1 would not like to take the responsibility of allowing seed such as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cockshutt) speaks of, to be distributed among the farmers for another year.

As an agriculturist, I think we have been too long without this Act, and I protest against it being postponed any longer than the minister has stated. It is generally admitted in this country that the weed nuisance is becoming a very serious one, that many of our best farms are becoming polluted with foul weeds, and that tlie cost of farming these lands -is increased by the weed nuisance. Farmers are looking to the Minister of Agriculture to provide a remedy for this condition of affairs. Having listened to the debate, I must say, as a farmer, that I compliment the Minister of Agriculture on the steps he has taken, and I hope he will not longer delay in putting the law into proper condition and bringing it into

force in the interests of the farming community.

I would just say, in answer to the hon. gentleman (Mr. P. H. McKenzie) that the seed grown in the province of Ontario is among the best in the world, in spite of our having no such law as is now proposed. I speak particularly of red clover and alsike. Ontario seed of these kinds brings, as is well known, more than the American product, and more than most of the European product. That being the case, why do we need this Bill so urgently ? It is certainly not because our seed is inferior. We have a large quantity of good seed, but most of it is shipped abroad.

That is the very difficulty. We are exporting our best seed, and inferior and foul seeds are being sold to our own farmers. And, unfortunately, we have too many farmers who are willing to buy bad seed. We would like to have it put beyond the power of farmers to buy poor seed. This should be done in their own interest. I have noticed that the principal part of the opposition to this Bill has come from the lawyers and the seedsmen. I am astonished, in the first place, that the lawyers should object to the Bill. They say it is going to cause no end of lawsuits. Well, that would certainly be in their interest. As to the seed dealers, I think that when the law is working properly-as it will do before it is long in force-it will be found that it will not injure them at all. And it will greatly benefit the country in which we all take such an interest, and the prime industry of the country, the industry of agriculture.

I am delighted to know that such good seed is produced in this province. And if, as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cockshutt) says, there is such a great amount of splendid seed throughout the country, so much the better for the country at large, and so much the less danger of disaster to the holders of the seed. If the seed is good there is no danger of trouble.

I am surprised to hear an hon. gentleman talking about opposition to this Bill. It can only be explained on the ground that it comes from gentlemen who are new members of this House, and who fail to make the distinction between fair criticism and opposition. The life of parliament is criticism. It is unfair for any hon. gentleman to charge His Majesty's loyal opposition with having opposed a Bill simply because they have criticised its provisions. We have been endeavouring to help the minister to improve the Bill and make it workable. This we have been doing for the past three years, and I am happy to say that there has been Mr. P. H. McKENZIE.
a vast improvement in the Bill. I think the minister himself admits that there has been a great improvement, and I am sure he will give us credit for the assistance we have given. I believe that he looks at it differently from these other lion, gentlemen. There may be questions on which we disagree. For instance, there is the question of the time When the law should come into operation. But for my part, I am not prepared to give an opinion of that subject. My hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) may be correct. He knows the conditions of the trade, probably, even better than the Minister of Agriculture does. There is room in this case for a fair difference of opinion; and I am sure that the Minister of Agriculture will not say that my hon. friend from Brantford has opposed the Bill simply because he has suggested a later time for its coming into operation. In view of the improvement that has already been made, it might be worth while to wait and get a perfect Bill, and one thoroughly workable-for there seems to be great difference of opinion as to whether this Bill is workable or not. I am not opposing the Bill by any means. If it is a good law for the country, His Majesty's loyal opposition will stand by it. We are the guardians of the farmers' interests as much as are hon. gentlemen opposite. I believe we represent more farmers than they do. We have been the friends of the farmers and have advocated the farmers' interests in every matter, not merely in such measures as this, but in the general policy of the country, and in providing markets for the farmer. It is not reasonable to say that we are opposing the measure because we criticise it. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture will give us credit for having assisted materially in bringing the Bill into its present improved shape.

I am glad to give hon. gentlemen opposite, and especially the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson), an old friend whom I have seen in this House for many years, all the credit possible. But I would give him even more credit if he had not said so much about being the friend of the farmer. The hon. gentleman doth protest too much, methinks, I believe the farmer will realize that fact. We are not going to discuss the question as to who are the friends of the farmers ; the records of parliament and the records of legislation will prove that better than any protestations the hon. gentleman can make or I can make. But I am glad the hon. gentlemen opposite endorse the Bill which I have the honour to present to the House, and of helping through so far as it has gone. The principle of the Bill after all is the chief thing, and if we can get an unanimous endorsation of the principle of the Bill, I have no doubt the details can be threshed out and made workable by the combined common sense of the

members of this House. The Bill to day, while not so drastic as it was, is probably more to the taste of the people than when it was first introduced, and is more likely to be successful when passed. X trust that when this Bill becomes law and has been in force for a few years, the condition of affairs will be such that we will be able to pass a still more drastic measure, giving greater protection to the purchaser of seeds and greater protection to those who are engaged in the trade. I would be glad to be able to do that in the years to come as Minister of Agriculture.

I do not think it lies in the mouth of the Minister of Agriculture to charge me, during the time I have been in this House, now some sixteen or seventeen sessions, with having at any time failed to stand up in the interests of the farmers of this country. Perhaps the hon. gentleman can recollect the time when he opposed a measure in this House that was directly in the interest of the farmers, when he stood up against a measure that was intended to protect the butter interests of the farmers. That is something I cannot be charged with. The hon. gentleman would take half an hour to explain awav that little difficulty. I have (heard him try to do it, but to my mind he failed altogether in accomplishing his object.
It was all explained away in the elections of 1897.	.
It is hard to explain away a speech and harder to explain away a vote.

I am astonished to bear the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) say that he has improved this Bill by opposing it during all these years. I am sorry that we did not live with him, or he with us, in the days of the children of Israel, when Moses brought down the law on the mount. We would have heard the hon. gentleman cry out '* Wait Moses for a little while until the members of the opposition get a chance at this Bill, and you will see how they will improve it for you.
This is a new phase of the question. I do not know what kind of seeds they had in those days, I do not know what the hon. gentleman refers to.
Manna.
He must have an extraordinary idea of legislation. I do not know where he is getting a precedent in those olden days for what we are doing this afternoon. He has not been here all the afternoon.
Where was he ?

I don't know, perhaps he was out with Moses somewhere. He spoke about my opposing the measure. I never opposed the measure, I do not know
a gentleman on this side who has opposed it. The member for South Renfrew (Mr. A. A. Wright) does not seem to be able to draw a distinction between fair criticism and opposition. The proper way to deal with the Bill in this House is to criticise it. I am not like the hon. gentleman, who merely sits here to register everything that the government proposes, whether it is right or wrong. When the hon. gentleman does that, I do not consider he is acting in the interests of his constituents, because he is simply registering what another man does. I am glad to hear the Minister of Agriculture say that while this measure is not so drastic as the measure of previous sessions, he thinks it will be much more acceptable to the people, and can be more effectually enforced.
I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again, when we will take into consideration the various sections that we have not dealt with.

I would suggest to the hon. gentleman not to take this up in committee stage again for, say, about ten days. The discussion we have had will go out to the country through the press, and in the meantime we may receive certain suggestions which will serve to make the Bill even better than it is.

The hon. gentleman's suggestion is reasonable, but the business of the House may require that we take it up a little earlier.
Progress reported.
